problem:
Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable with respect to $t$ on $t\in (0,\pi )?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =⟨\operatorname{sin}⁡(2t),\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2-\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)⟩ \\ g(t) & =⟨1+{t}^{2},\,-t+2,\,\sqrt{t}⟩ \\ h(t) & =⟨\frac{1}{t},\,\operatorname{tan}⁡t,\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t⟩\end{aligned}
$$

choices.value: All of them are differentiable on $(0,\pi )$
None of them are differentiable on $(0,\pi )$

activity_context.topic_title: Continuity and Differentiability of Vector-Valued Functions

feedback.problem:
Which of the following vector-valued functions are differentiable at $t=1?$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(t) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+|t-1|\,j+(2t+1)\,k \\ g(t) & =\frac{2}{t}\,i+{t}^{3}\,j+\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,k \\ h(t) & =2t\,i+\operatorname{csc}⁡(\pi t)\,j+{t}^{4}\,k\end{aligned}
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A vector-valued function is differentiable at a point if and only if each of its components is differentiable at that point. 

Let's consider the functions one-by-one. 

- The derivative of the second component $|t-1|$ of $f(t)$ is not defined at $t=1.$ So, we conclude that $f(t)$ is not differentiable at this point.

- Next, we differentiate $g(t)$  to find ${g}^{′}(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{g}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{2}{t})\,i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({t}^{3})\,j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,k \\  & =-\frac{2}{{t}^{2}}\,i+3{t}^{2}\,j+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

Since each component of ${g}^{′}(t)$ is defined   at $t=1$, we conclude that $g(t)$ is differentiable at this point.

- Finally, the  second component $\operatorname{csc}⁡(\pi t)$ of  $h(t)$ is not defined at $t=1.$ So, we conclude that $h(t)$ is not differentiable at this point.

Therefore, the correct answer is "$g(t)$ only."
